claims.text: Sliding-induced dynamic amorphization creates an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer in HEA protective coatings.
The ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer triggers inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer enhances wear resistance.
The initial HEA coating has a coarse-grained microstructure.
The initial coating is homogeneous and has this microstructure in its as-deposited state.
Varying sliding load or speed can be used to trigger dynamic amorphization.
An inert environment minimizes oxidation during sliding.
A load-and-speed regime has been shown to induce dynamic amorphization without excessive thermal degradation.
Localized stress and shear initiate amorphization at the sliding surface.
The amorphized surface rapidly recrystallizes into an ultra-nanocrystalline structure.
Grain refinement in the inverse Hall-Petch regime lowers shear strength.
Coatings subjected to the proposed sliding treatment will have a lower friction coefficient than coarse-microstructure controls.
Coatings subjected to the proposed sliding treatment will have a lower wear rate than coarse-microstructure controls.
TEM or STEM will reveal a refined ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer in treated specimens.
Coarse-grained coatings that do not undergo the controlled sliding treatment retain their original microstructure and exhibit higher friction and wear.
The proposed mechanism applies only when sliding conditions activate dynamic amorphization and may fail under highly oxidative or insufficient-stress conditions.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as not subjected to the controlled sliding conditions, yet friction and wear are to be compared under similar or identical conditions. A specimen cannot remain unslid and simultaneously provide directly comparable sliding-friction and wear measurements; a common test followed by demonstrably different microstructural evolution is needed.
The control is described as being maintained under identical conditions while also receiving insufficient sliding force or speed, even though load and speed are the controlled intervention variables.
